messages.author: 7a5d15676a9d8586
messages.subject: DSM and "weights" argument
parts:
Good afternoon wonderful distance sampling group,

I am creating a dsm with line transect data for a species of alpine songbird. These data were collected in extremely rugged terrain and the line transects are not straight lines within an alpine basin, they follow the curvature of the basin, sampling across a habitat suitability gradient, so "good", "marginal", and "bad" habitat are all represented. Because some assumptions are relaxed using a dsm (like non-randomly placed lines) we decided to use this modeling method, as well as wanting to draw ecological inference about a species with little available information.
I am curious about the "weights" argument that can be included in the dsm modeling. Because of the rugged alpine terrain, transects are not uniform in size, shape, and area. So I have a column in my "segdata" data frame (with information about line transect segments) that is the area surveyed for each line transect segment.
My questions are these:
1. How is the "weights" argument used in the dsm (when not specified in the model). It seems from the dsm R Documentation page (?dsm) that when weights is not included in the model, it is set to weights = NULL, which would assume that all line transect segments were the same length and covered the same area. Is that correct? Or does the model calculate the surveyed area (as 2 * truncation distance * Effort (line segment length) from the "segdata" dataframe?
2. In what context is it appropriate to use the "weights" argument and specify the actual surveyed area of the line transect segment? I wasn't sure if this is an appropriate argument to include if I'm using "count" as the response. May I use the "weights" argument with my area column (from segdata) specified with the "count" as response or is it only appropriate to use with "abundance.est" as the response?
3. When I did include the weights=segdata$segment.area call in my dsm (with count as the response), my deviance explained went from 36% (no weights argument) to 56.5% (weights argument specified), and all variables were suddenly extremely significant (all p-value = <2e-16), whereas in the model without weights  the p-values had a wide range of values (from 0.049 to <2e-16). Why would the deviance explained shoot up so drastically and p-values all drop to <2e-16? 
*Obviously, if it is inappropriate to use "weights" in the count as response model, I don't need to worry about this, I just need to remove the term.
4. I am also not clear when it is appropriate to use "count" as the response vs. "abundance.est" vs. "density.est" for response variable. My detection function did not improve by including covariates, and from what I have read I could use either "count" or "abundance.est", but I am not clear on when or why I would use the different model responses. Also, do I need to format the input data in the "segdata" file differently for each of these response types?

Thank you for your time and energy answering these questions or providing articles or other scholarly materials for me to review.
Warm regards,
Kat Bernier  
PhD candidate
University of California, Santa Cruz

messages.author: 75e0b0abcbafbc7d
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] DSM and "weights" argument
parts:
Kat

I'll address your questions by the numbers you used in your email:
  1. weights is only used when the response variable is density; as you suggested, in other situations sampled area is 2w*seglength
  2. in nearly all circumstances, you will not use the weights argument. The offset (used in the gam model) is calculated automatically
  3. weights is not used when response variable is count
  4. choice between count and abundance.est as response variable is determined by whether individual level covariates are included in the detection function model. Individual level covariates examples: species or sex of detected animal. When those covariates are not in the detection function model, use count as response.
The choice of response variables is discussed in the dsm case study section on model fitting. Discussion of the use of the weights argument is found in this section of help for dsm
Fit a density surface model to segment-specific estimates of abundance or density. — dsm • dsm
Details. The response (LHS of formula) can be one of the following (with restrictions outlined below):. count count in each segment. abundance.est estimated abundance per segment, estimation is via a Horvitz-Thompson estimator. density.est density per segment. The offset used in the model is dependent on the response: count area of segment multiplied by average probability of detection in the ...

parts:
Thank you for your quick response and the resources, Eric!
It sounds like using the "weights" argument does not apply to my situation.

A couple of follow-up questions that I have (after reviewing the linked materials):
1. In what occasion is the "density.est" response used? I was still not clear from the case study or the help page descriptions. I feel clear about the use of "count" and "abundance.est" as response, but still do not understand how or when "density.est" is used as a response.

2. Is the data formatted differently when the response is "density.est"? For example, would I need to calculate the density per transect segment (from the detection function and presumably using the actual count data) and add a column in the segdata?

3. If I am using "count" as the response, is it appropriate to specify the segment.area in my model function? My line transect segments are NOT uniform in area because they follow the natural curvature of an alpine basin, thus the upper transect line has a greater area than the lower transect lines. I understand that the default segment.area calculation is by using the column "Effort" * 2 * truncation distance, but this would not capture the variation in my line transect segment areas.
For example, my dsm code may look like this:
dsm_tw_haz_109 <- dsm(count~s(Elev, bs="ts", k=10)+
                                     s(HeatLoad, bs="ts",k=20)+
                                     s(CliffPerc, bs= "ts", k= 10)+
                                     s(NDVI2019, bs="ts", k=20)+
                                     s(JuneMinT,bs="ts", k=20)+
                                     s(AdjMeadowP,bs="ts", k=10),
                               ddf.obj=BCRF.haz.109.bin15m,
                               segment.data = segdata2019,
                               segment.area=segdata2019$segment.area,
                               observation.data=obs_sf,
                               family=tw())

Thank you again for your dedication to this list serve! It is extremely beneficial to us less experienced distance sampling modelers.

Warm holiday regards,
Kat Bernier
PhD Candidate

messages.author: 75e0b0abcbafbc7d
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] DSM and "weights" argument
parts:
Kat:

Using density as a response in density surface modelling is uncommon; I can't think of an example where it has appeared in the literature. I suggest keeping with count as your response variable.

As you note, the dsm function has a segment.area argument. It can be used in your situation where there is not symmetry in your segment geometry. As the dsm documentation states, if the segment.area argument is provided, it overrides the segment area calculation within the function.
